new_statements.quote: Stress is about even on all syllables, with these noticeable exceptions (vowels strongly stressed are capitalised; excrescent vowels with weak stress are shown with a brev): (1) CVCV words seem stressed on the final vowels: hanA hibiscus flower, kiyÓ outrigger boom, yifA? where?, YisÓ Esau, yiwE then. (2) Syllables beginning with h- are usually stressed: yapwahAaló to dry out, pahAló to drift away, yekúhÚ rak just a little. (3) The excrescent vowel is weak and unstressed (except after h-). [...] (e) A number of words of the shape C1V1C2V2C3V3 have stress on V1 and V3 and weak stress on V2: TilĭmE male name, yefŏmA a tree.
new_statements.citation: Elbert, Samuel H. 1974. Puluwat Grammar. Pacific Linguistics, Series B, No. 29. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

(2) Syllables beginning with h- are usually stressed: yapwahAaló to dry out, pahAló to drift away, yekúhÚ rak just a little. (3) The excrescent vowel is weak and unstressed (except after h-).. new_statements.rule_in_words: No strongly culminative word stress: syllables are roughly evenly stressed. Where differences are noted they favour the word-final vowel (CVCV -> final; CVCVCV -> first and third vowels strong, second weak, i.e. final plus alternate preceding), any syllable with onset h-, and never the excrescent (epenthetic) vowel unless it follows h-. Author hedges ('seem', 'usually').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not named as such; item (e) gives two strong vowels (V1 and V3) in trisyllables with weak V2, which reads as an alternating pattern anchored at the final vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: h-initial syllables attract stress regardless of position; excrescent vowels are unstressed except after h-; p.111 notes the conjunction nge 'but' is weakly stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level 'Notes on Stress' on citation forms, kept separate by the author from the following utterance-level 'Notes on Pitch and Juncture' (pp.14-15). IDENTITY CAVEAT: the statement describes the speech of Puluwat atoll (Glottolog nucl1478 under pulu1242), not Pollap; it is extended to Pollapese only on the basis that Pollap speech is treated as a dialect of the same language (Lynch 2002 p.804; Ethnologue puw; Glottolog pula1265). This exact statement is already in our catalog under pulu1242 (qs-tier 2026-09-12, classification not determinable).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog double-lists Pollap speech: poll1238 'Pollapese' (language-level, sister of Puluwatese under the 'Puluatese' node, sole ref Crippen 2009) and pula1265 'Pulapese' (dialect of Puluwatese pulu1242, ISO puw). The only first-hand stress statement found (Elbert 1974) describes Puluwat atoll speech (nucl1478/pulu1242) and is already catalogued under pulu1242; applying it to poll1238 would be an editorial dialect-extension, not a Pollapese-specific record. No source describing Pollap/Pollapese speech itself was obtainable.

sources.note: pp.13-14 'Notes on Stress': stress about even on all syllables, except CVCV words seem stressed on the final vowel, h-initial syllables usually stressed, excrescent vowels weak/unstressed (except after h-), and C1V1C2V2C3V3 words stressed on V1 and V3 with weak V2. Describes Puluwat atoll speech (informant Tilime); Pulap/Pollap not named. Already in our catalog under pulu1242.
Paraphrases Elbert 1974: syllables stressed fairly evenly; final vowels in CVCV words stressed; syllables after h stressed; names Pulapese and Pulusukese as dialects. Tertiary.

sources.citation: Lynch, John. 2002. Puluwatese [grammar sketch abstracted from Elbert 1974]. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds), The Oceanic Languages, 804-814. Richmond: Curzon.
sources.note: p.804 says the language is spoken on Puluwat, Pulap and Pulusuk; p.805 sec.1.3 'Stress is about even on all syllables, except that it falls more heavily on the final syllable in words of the form CVCV, and also on any syllable beginning with /h/; the excrescent vowel.. is unstressed unless preceded by /h/.' Second-hand from Elbert 1974.
